ABV: Alcohol by volume: the estimated percentage of the finished beer that is alcohol. BrewMaster calculates it from original and final gravity using the more detailed ABV formula. It is a prediction until you enter measured gravities.
Bitterness: IBU means International Bitterness Units. BrewMaster uses the Tinseth formula with hop amount, alpha acids, time and wort gravity. Perceived bitterness also depends on sweetness and body; dry hops add zero IBU in this model.
Color: SRM is a beer color scale: lower values are pale and higher values are darker. Morey estimates SRM from fermentable amounts and malt colors; EBC is another color scale. The swatch is an approximation, not a flavor or clarity measurement.
Original gravity: OG is the wort's density before fermentation, compared with water at 1.000. For example, 1.050 means 50 gravity points. More extract raises OG and the potential alcohol, depending on how much the yeast ferments.
Final gravity: FG is the beer's density after fermentation. BrewMaster estimates it from yeast attenuation, mash temperature and the fermentables. It helps estimate alcohol and body, but is not a direct sweetness measurement.
ABV · standard: The standard estimate is (OG − FG) × 131.25. It is shown for comparison; the main ABV display uses the more detailed formula. Both rely on predicted gravities until measurements are entered.
ABV · accurate: The more detailed estimate is [76.08 × (OG − FG) ÷ (1.775 − OG)] × (FG ÷ 0.794). It accounts for gravity differently from the standard formula, but still depends on the quality of the OG and FG inputs.
BU:GU: Bitterness units divided by original gravity points. A beer at 40 IBU and OG 1.050 has a BU:GU of 0.80. Use it as a rough balance comparison; yeast, roast, final gravity and hop aroma also change how bitterness tastes.
Calories: An approximate serving calorie estimate from original and final gravity, accounting for alcohol and residual extract. It is not a nutritional analysis. Additive effects such as fruit, cocoa or spirits are outside this model.
Pre-boil gravity: Estimated wort density before evaporation concentrates it during the boil. BrewMaster distributes the recipe's gravity points across the calculated pre-boil volume, assuming those points are conserved.
Pre-boil volume: Wort needed at the start of the boil: post-boil batch volume plus boil-off rate × boil duration. Starting water also needs to cover grain absorption; see the water planner for that estimate.
Cells to pitch: The estimated yeast cells to add. The baseline is 0.75 million cells per mL per degree Plato for ale, or 1.5 million for lager, multiplied by your pitch multiplier. Actual needs depend on yeast health and handling.
Attenuation: Apparent attenuation describes how much of the original gravity points disappear during fermentation. Higher attenuation generally lowers FG. The recipe estimate adjusts the strain midpoint for mash temperature and fermentable type; it does not model a complete fermentation.
Grist: The grain bill is the full fermentable mixture. A grist percentage is this ingredient's weight divided by the total fermentable weight. These percentages are weight shares, not shares of fermentable sugar.
Malt color: Degrees Lovibond (°L) and EBC describe malt color. They are ingredient specs; the finished beer's color also depends on the amount used and batch volume. A small amount of dark malt can change beer color substantially.
Potential: PPG means gravity points per pound per US gallon at full extraction. A 36 PPG ingredient could yield SG 1.036 from 1 lb in 1 US gal at 100% extraction. Mash-required ingredients are reduced by your efficiency in the recipe calculation.
Extract percent: The extract yield listed or converted for this fermentable, expressed as a percentage. It describes potential extract, not your equipment efficiency and not the percentage of the beer that will become alcohol.
Diastatic power: An indicator of the malt's starch-converting enzyme activity, expressed here in degrees Lintner. It helps assess mash conversion. This unit is different from degrees Lovibond, which measures color.
Requires mash: Mash-required ingredients use your efficiency in the gravity estimate. Extract and other non-mash fermentables count at full potential. Steeping alone does not perform the same starch conversion as a mash.
Max grist: The recommended maximum weight share of this ingredient in the fermentable bill. It guides ingredient selection and solver penalties. If no published limit is known, the app identifies its model cap instead of presenting it as a manufacturer limit.
Alpha acids: Alpha acids are hop compounds used in the bitterness calculation. AA % is their percentage by weight. Use the value on your actual hop package when available because harvest and storage can differ from the catalog range.
Beta acids: Another measured hop acid fraction. It is stored as a reference spec; BrewMaster's Tinseth IBU calculation uses alpha acids and does not separately model beta-acid oxidation.
Cohumulone: One component of a hop's alpha acids, listed as a percentage of total alpha acids. It is a reference spec here and is not a separate bitterness adjustment in the calculation engine.
Total oils: The hop's measured total oil content in mL per 100 g. The flavor model uses it as one scaling input, along with dose and timing. More oil does not guarantee a stronger or better aroma in a finished beer.
Oil breakdown: The reported shares of individual hop oils, where known. Oil chemistry helps compare hops, but it does not directly measure a beer's aroma. Missing values mean unknown, not zero.
Alcohol tolerance: The approximate alcohol level a strain can tolerate under suitable conditions. It is not the ABV the yeast automatically produces: wort gravity, fermentability and fermentation performance determine the result.
ABV at entered OG: An estimate from your entered wort OG and the strain's midpoint attenuation. It compares strains at the same starting gravity and is separate from alcohol tolerance. It does not include a specific recipe's mash or grain adjustments.
Flocculation: How readily yeast cells gather together and settle. Higher flocculation usually means faster settling; lower flocculation can leave yeast suspended longer. It does not tell you how much sugar the strain will ferment.
Temperature: The strain's catalog fermentation range. Use it as a starting guide and check the lab's product sheet for your culture. Fermentation temperature affects performance and the app's subjective ester and phenol estimates.
POF: Phenolic off-flavor status. POF-positive strains can make phenolic aromas such as clove; that character is welcome in some beer styles. A negative result does not mean the strain has no other flavor character.
Diastaticus: A yeast designation associated with the ability to break down some dextrins and ferment further. Check the culture lab's current strain information. BrewMaster's simple FG model does not simulate this extended fermentation process.
Consensus: A subjective combination of descriptor records that match the usage context, weighted by source type and confidence. Scores run from 0 to 5. Confidence is an editorial assessment, not a laboratory measurement or statistical certainty.
Mash temperature: The temperature of the grain-and-water mash. In this model, cooler mashes increase estimated fermentability and warmer mashes decrease it. This is a simplified attenuation adjustment; enzyme activity and mash schedules are more complex.
Mash duration: How long the mash is held, recorded in minutes for your brew process. BrewMaster does not currently model how mash duration changes starch conversion or efficiency.
Fermentation temperature: The planned fermentation temperature. The flavor model uses it to shift the chosen yeast's estimated ester and phenol contributions. It does not by itself change the recipe's numeric attenuation estimate.
Pitch multiplier: Scales the calculated yeast cell requirement. 1× uses the ale or lager baseline; 1.5× requests 50% more cells. It also influences the model's subjective yeast flavor estimate, not OG or the numeric FG calculation.
Carbonation: Volumes of CO₂: the amount of dissolved carbon dioxide relative to the beer volume. Higher values mean more carbonation. This setting informs the structure estimate and brew plan; it does not calculate priming sugar or serving pressure.
Whirlpool utilization factor: The fraction of calculated boil-style hop utilization used for whirlpool additions. For example, 0.15 means 15%. Set it lower for cooler contact or use your own observations. This simplified factor does not simulate whirlpool temperature or cooling.
Hop minutes: For boil additions, minutes remaining before the boil ends. For whirlpool additions, planned hot contact time. Longer hot contact raises the calculated utilization; a whirlpool reduction factor also applies.
Hop days: Planned dry-hop contact time in days. Dry hops contribute zero IBU in this model; dose, timing context and oils influence the subjective aroma estimate. Contact time remains part of your brew schedule.
Post-boil batch size: Wort volume after the boil, before transfer loss. Changing this setting scales the recipe's ingredient quantities. Packaged beer will be lower after transfer and packaging losses.
Brewhouse efficiency: The percentage of mash-required fermentables' potential gravity recovered into the planned batch. It defaults to 72%. Changing it in the editor rescales those fermentables to preserve gravity; extract and sugar are counted at full potential.
Boil duration: Total planned boil time. Together with boil-off rate, it determines the pre-boil volume. Hop addition times are separate entries and remain editable when this changes.
Boil-off rate: Volume evaporated per hour on your equipment. BrewMaster multiplies it by boil duration to estimate the extra pre-boil wort needed. Measure your own kettle to improve this setting.
Transfer loss: Wort left behind when moving from kettle to fermenter, such as kettle trub or tubing losses. It reduces the estimated fermenter volume. Packaging loss is a separate setting in the water planner.
Minimum alcohol tolerance: Filter strains by their catalog alcohol tolerance. Unknown tolerances are excluded when you set a minimum. This limit is separate from the beer's predicted ABV.
Personal source weight: How heavily your own ingredient tasting notes count in subjective flavor consensus, from 1× to 3×. It does not change objective ingredient specs or brewing formulas. Enable personal notes to include this layer.
Personal descriptor intensity: Your perceived intensity for the selected ingredient descriptor, from 0 (absent) to 5 (very strong). It becomes a user tasting record with its usage context. It is an opinion layer, separate from measured gravity and volume.
Calibration: Uses your measured brew logs to estimate equipment efficiency and a per-yeast attenuation baseline. Estimates account for the recipe's mash and grist assumptions. A small sample can reflect measurement error or unusual conditions.
Dry packet size: The mass of yeast in one dry packet, used to turn the cell requirement into an estimated packet count. The planner's cells-per-gram assumption is editable; check the yeast supplier's pitch instructions.
Style check: Compares calculated OG, FG, ABV, IBU and color with the selected style's legacy numeric ranges. These ranges are a reference, not a judgment of beer quality. They do not change your recipe or prevent manual edits.
Grain bill: The fermentables and amounts that provide the beer's extract, color and part of its body and flavor. Numeric specs drive the brewing calculations; contextual flavor descriptors drive the separate sensory estimate.
Hop schedule: Each hop addition has a variety, amount, use and contact time. Early boil additions favor calculated bitterness; late boil, whirlpool and dry-hop contexts have different aroma weights in the subjective model.
Brew-day numbers: These values are deterministic calculations from the recipe and selected assumptions. They are predictions until checked against measurements. Flavor scores and perceived balance remain separate subjective estimates.
